_about: Objects for the Cosmic Scale page (scale.html). size = the quoted length in metres (what it measures is in 'what'); w/h = the box the drawing occupies, in metres (defaults to size). Every size carries a source. Compiled September 2026. Geographic outlines (geo.la, geo.earthMask) are derived from Natural Earth 1:10m and 1:50m land polygons (public domain) via the world-atlas npm package.

objects.name: Proton
objects.text: Three quarks held together by gluons. Its charge radius is 0.841 femtometres (fm), and most of its mass comes from the energy of the gluon field rather than from the quarks themselves.

src.label: CODATA 2022 proton rms charge radius, NIST

objects.name: Uranium-238 nucleus
objects.text: 92 protons and 146 neutrons packed like marbles in a bag. Nuclear radius grows as 1.2 fm × A^(1/3); matter this dense would put about a billion tonnes in a teaspoon.

src.label: Nuclear radius R = 1.2 fm·A^(1/3): K. S. Krane, Introductory Nuclear Physics (Wiley, 1988); HyperPhysics

objects.name: Gamma-ray wavelength
objects.text: Gamma rays from radioactive nuclei and cosmic explosions have wavelengths around a picometre (pm), a hundred times smaller than an atom. That is why they pass through matter so easily.

src.label: NASA Science, Tour of the Electromagnetic Spectrum: Gamma Rays

objects.name: Hydrogen atom
objects.text: One proton and one electron. The electron is not a ball on an orbit but a cloud of probability, densest at the centre; the nucleus is about 63,000 times narrower than the atom.

src.label: CODATA 2022 Bohr radius a₀ = 52.9 pm, NIST

objects.name: Water molecule
objects.text: Two hydrogens on an oxygen, 104.5° apart. A glass of water holds about 10²⁵ molecules, more than the estimated number of stars in the observable universe.

src.label: Properties of water: O–H 95.84 pm, H–O–H 104.45°

objects.name: Buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀)
objects.text: Sixty carbon atoms in the pattern of a football: 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons. Discovered in 1985 while simulating the atmospheres of carbon stars, and found in space in 2010.

src.label: Kroto et al. 1985, Nature 318, 162; Cami et al. 2010, Science 329, 1180

objects.name: DNA double helix
objects.text: The double helix is 2 nanometres (nm) wide and makes one full turn every 3.4 nm. Unwound, the DNA in a single human cell would stretch about 2 metres.

src.label: Watson & Crick 1953, Nature 171, 737

objects.name: Ribosome
objects.text: The protein factory of every cell. It reads messenger RNA and links amino acids together, a few per second; a human cell holds millions of them.

src.label: Anger et al. 2013, Structures of the human and Drosophila 80S ribosome, Nature 497, 80

objects.name: Coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2)
objects.text: A fatty envelope studded with spike proteins around one strand of RNA about 30,000 letters long. Smaller than the wavelength of visible light, so no ordinary microscope can resolve it.

src.label: Zhu et al. 2020, New England Journal of Medicine 382, 727

objects.name: Wavelength of green light
objects.text: Visible light spans about 380 to 750 nm; our eyes are most sensitive near 555 nm. A light microscope cannot separate details much smaller than about half this length.

src.label: NASA Science, Tour of the Electromagnetic Spectrum: Visible Light

objects.name: E. coli bacterium
objects.text: A rod about 2 micrometres (µm) long that swims by spinning its whip-like flagella. Your gut holds roughly as many bacteria as your body has human cells.

src.label: Milo & Phillips, Cell Biology by the Numbers; Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, PLOS Biology

objects.name: Red blood cell
objects.text: You carry about 25 trillion of them. The dimpled disc can fold to squeeze through capillaries narrower than itself, and each one lives about 120 days.

src.label: Sender, Fuchs & Milo 2016, Revised estimates for the number of human and bacteria cells in the body, PLOS Biology

objects.name: Human egg cell
objects.text: The largest cell in the human body, about 0.12 millimetres (mm) across: just at the limit of what the naked eye can see.

src.label: Milo & Phillips, Cell Biology by the Numbers: How big are human cells?

objects.name: Human hair
objects.text: A strand of keratin wrapped in overlapping cuticle scales, typically 50 to 100 µm thick. Hundreds of red blood cells could lie across its end.

src.label: C. R. Robbins, Chemical and Physical Behavior of Human Hair (Springer, 2012)

objects.name: Grain of sand
objects.text: Geologists call a grain 'sand' if it is between 1/16 mm and 2 mm; this is a medium grain of quartz, worn round by water and wind.

src.label: Wentworth 1922, A scale of grade and class terms for clastic sediments, Journal of Geology 30, 377

objects.name: Garden ant
objects.text: A black garden ant worker (Lasius niger) is 3 to 5 mm long. There are roughly 20 quadrillion ants on Earth, about 2.5 million for every person.

src.label: AntWiki: Lasius niger; Schultheiss et al. 2022, PNAS 119, e2201550119

objects.name: Honeybee
objects.text: A worker honeybee is about 12 to 15 mm long and beats its wings around 230 times per second.

src.label: M. L. Winston, The Biology of the Honey Bee (Harvard University Press, 1987)

objects.name: Football (soccer ball)
objects.text: A size-5 ball is 68–70 cm around, so about 22 cm across. Its 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons are exactly the pattern of the C₆₀ molecule, 220 million times smaller.

src.label: International Football Association Board (IFAB), Laws of the Game, Law 2: The Ball

objects.name: Human
objects.text: You. Adult height averages about 1.7 m worldwide. On the ruler you sit about 15 powers of ten above a proton and 27 below the edge of the observable universe.

src.label: NCD Risk Factor Collaboration 2016, A century of trends in adult human height, eLife 5, e13410

objects.name: Blue whale
objects.text: The largest animal ever known to have lived: typically 25 m long and up to about 150 tonnes. Its heart is the size of a small car.

src.label: NOAA Fisheries: Blue Whale

objects.name: Space Shuttle Endeavour
objects.text: 37.24 m long with a 23.79 m wingspan, seen here from above. Endeavour flew 25 missions from 1992 to 2011 and now stands at the California Science Center in Los Angeles.

src.label: NASA, Flights of Endeavour (OV-105); Wikipedia, Space Shuttle orbiter

objects.name: Statue of Liberty
objects.text: 93 m from the ground to the torch; the copper statue itself is 46 m, standing on a 27 m pedestal and a 20 m star-shaped fort.

src.label: U.S. National Park Service, Statue Statistics

objects.name: Saturn V rocket
objects.text: The Moon rocket: 110.6 m tall and 2,900 tonnes when fuelled. Thirteen flew between 1967 and 1973, carrying 24 astronauts to the Moon.

src.label: NASA MSFC, Saturn V Flight Evaluation Report AS-506 (1969); Wikipedia, Saturn V

objects.name: Burj Khalifa
objects.text: The tallest building on Earth since 2010, in Dubai. Its 163 floors and spire reach 828 m; the top is about 6 °C cooler than the street.

src.label: Council on Tall Buildings and Urban Habitat (CTBUH), Skyscraper Center: Burj Khalifa

objects.name: Mount Everest
objects.text: 8,848.86 m, measured by a joint Nepal–China survey in 2020. The air pressure at the summit is about a third of that at sea level.

src.label: Nepal–China joint survey, announced 8 December 2020 (National Geographic)

objects.name: Los Angeles Basin
objects.what: across (Santa Monica Mountains to San Joaquin Hills)
objects.text: A lowland of sediment ringed by mountains and home to millions of people, seen at night from Santa Monica Bay to the harbour at San Pedro. Coastline from Natural Earth; the city lights are illustrative.

src.label: Natural Earth 1:10m coastline (public domain); USGS Los Angeles Coastal Plain

objects.name: Grand Canyon
objects.text: 446 km long, up to 29 km wide and 1.8 km deep. The Colorado River has exposed nearly two billion years of rock in its walls.

src.label: U.S. National Park Service, Grand Canyon Park Statistics

objects.name: International Space Station orbit
objects.text: The International Space Station (ISS) circles about 410 km up, once every 93 minutes. On a globe the size of a basketball, that is less than 8 mm above the surface.

src.label: NASA, International Space Station Facts and Figures

objects.name: The Moon
objects.text: 3,474.8 km across, a little over a quarter of Earth. Twelve people have walked on it.

src.label: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

objects.name: Earth
objects.text: 12,742 km across. Nearly all of its air lies within about 30 km of the ground: shrink Earth to an apple and the atmosphere would be thinner than the peel.

src.label: NASA Earth Fact Sheet (NSSDCA); coastlines: Natural Earth

objects.name: Jupiter
objects.text: The largest planet, 11 Earths across and more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth.

src.label: NASA Jupiter Fact Sheet (NSSDCA)

objects.name: Earth–Moon distance
objects.text: 384,400 km on average, about 30 Earth diameters. At the Moon's farthest, all seven other planets could line up in the gap.

src.label: NASA Moon Fact Sheet (NSSDCA): semi-major axis, apogee 405,696 km

objects.name: The Sun
objects.text: 1.39 million km across: 109 Earths, or a million Earths by volume. It holds 99.86% of the Solar System's mass.

src.label: IAU 2015 Resolution B3 nominal solar radius; NASA Sun Fact Sheet

objects.name: Arcturus
objects.text: The brightest star in the northern sky is an orange giant 25 times the Sun's radius, 37 light-years away. It is roughly what the Sun will become in about 5 billion years.

src.label: Ramírez & Allende Prieto 2011, ApJ 743, 135

objects.name: Earth's orbit (1 AU)
objects.text: One astronomical unit (AU), exactly 149,597,870,700 m, is Earth's average distance from the Sun. Sunlight takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to cross it.

src.label: IAU 2012 Resolution B2 (definition of the AU)

objects.name: Betelgeuse
objects.text: The red shoulder of Orion, about 550 light-years away. Put in place of the Sun, its surface would reach past the orbit of Mars and beyond the asteroid belt.

src.label: Joyce et al. 2020, ApJ 902, 63

objects.name: VY Canis Majoris
objects.text: A red hypergiant about 3,800 light-years away and one of the largest stars known. The best current measurement, by interferometry, gives 1,420 solar radii: in place of the Sun, its surface would lie beyond Jupiter's orbit.

src.label: Wittkowski et al. 2012, A&A 540, L12 (1,420 ± 120 R☉)

objects.name: Neptune's orbit
objects.text: The eight planets, placed where they are today (circular-orbit approximation). Neptune circles at 30 AU; sunlight takes over four hours to get there.

src.label: NASA Planetary Fact Sheet; JPL Keplerian elements (Standish)

objects.name: Voyager 1 & the heliopause
objects.text: Voyager 1 left the Sun's bubble of solar wind, the heliopause, at 121.6 AU in 2012. On 18 November 2026 it becomes the first spacecraft one light-day (173.1 AU) from Earth.

src.label: NASA Science, Where Are Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 Now?; EarthSky, 26 June 2026

objects.name: Sedna's orbit
objects.text: A dwarf planet on an 11,400-year orbit that swings from 76 AU out to about 937 AU. Nobody knows for sure what flung it so far.

src.label: JPL Small-Body Database: 90377 Sedna

objects.name: One light-year
objects.what: distance light travels in a Julian year
objects.text: 9.46 trillion km, or 63,241 AU: the distance light covers in one year. It is a unit of distance, not of time.

src.label: International Astronomical Union (IAU): Measuring the Universe

objects.name: Oort cloud
objects.text: A vast, never-seen shell of icy bodies thought to begin a few thousand AU out and reach perhaps 100,000 AU, the source of long-period comets.

src.label: NASA Science: Oort Cloud

objects.name: Distance to Alpha Centauri
objects.text: The nearest star system: Alpha Centauri A and B at 4.37 light-years, with the red dwarf Proxima slightly closer at 4.24. At Voyager 1's speed the trip would take about 77,000 years.

src.label: Kervella et al. 2016, A&A 594, A107

objects.name: Orion Nebula
objects.text: A star nursery 1,350 light-years away, 24 light-years across, lit by the hot young stars of the Trapezium. Visible to the naked eye in Orion's sword.

src.label: Menten et al. 2007, A&A 474, 515 (distance 414 pc)

objects.name: Pleiades
objects.text: The Seven Sisters: over a thousand young stars 444 light-years away, still wrapped in a passing cloud of blue reflecting dust. The cluster is about 86 light-years across.

src.label: Adams et al. 2001, AJ 121, 2053; Gaia Collaboration 2018, A&A 616, A10

objects.name: Omega Centauri
objects.text: The Milky Way's biggest globular cluster: about 10 million ancient stars in a ball 150 light-years wide, possibly the core of a swallowed dwarf galaxy.

src.label: Wikipedia, Omega Centauri (after Harris 2010 catalogue)

objects.name: Large Magellanic Cloud
objects.text: A satellite galaxy of the Milky Way, 162,000 light-years away and visible from the Southern Hemisphere as a detached piece of the Milky Way.

src.label: Pietrzyński et al. 2019, Nature 567, 200 (49.59 kpc)

objects.name: Milky Way
objects.text: Our galaxy: 100 to 400 billion stars in a barred spiral disk about 100,000 light-years across. The Sun sits 26,700 light-years from the central black hole.

src.label: GRAVITY Collaboration 2019, A&A 625, L10 (R₀ = 8.178 kpc)

objects.name: Andromeda Galaxy
objects.text: The nearest big galaxy, with about a trillion stars. It is approaching at about 110 km/s, and the two galaxies may merge several billion years from now.

src.label: van der Marel et al. 2012, ApJ 753, 8

objects.name: Distance to Andromeda
objects.text: 2.5 million light-years. The light reaching your eyes from Andromeda tonight set off before our species existed.

src.label: Li et al. 2021, ApJ 920, 84 (761 kpc)

objects.name: Local Group
objects.text: Our galactic neighbourhood: the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum and more than 80 small galaxies held together by gravity.

src.label: McConnachie 2012, AJ 144, 4

objects.name: Virgo Cluster
objects.text: About 1,500 galaxies 54 million light-years away, anchored by the giant elliptical M87, whose black hole was the first ever imaged.

src.label: Mei et al. 2007, ApJ 655, 144; Wikipedia, Virgo Cluster

objects.name: Boötes Void
objects.text: A vast, nearly empty bubble 330 million light-years across. As astronomer Greg Aldering put it, had the Milky Way sat at its centre, we would not have known other galaxies existed until the 1960s.

src.label: Kirshner et al. 1981, ApJ 248, L57

objects.name: Laniakea Supercluster
objects.text: 'Immense heaven' in Hawaiian: about 100,000 galaxies whose motions all flow toward the Great Attractor. The Milky Way lies near its edge.

src.label: Tully, Courtois, Hoffman & Pomarède 2014, Nature 513, 71

objects.name: Cosmic web
objects.what: width of this slice (2.2 billion ly)
objects.text: On the largest scales, galaxies lie along filaments and sheets around enormous voids, the pattern gravity grew from tiny ripples in the early universe.

src.label: Springel et al. 2005, the Millennium Simulation, Nature 435, 629

objects.name: Observable universe
objects.text: Everything whose light has had time to reach us. It is 93 billion light-years across, even though the universe is 13.8 billion years old, because space kept expanding while the light travelled.

src.label: Planck Collaboration 2020, A&A 641, A6 (cosmological parameters)

tour.text: This is you: about 1.7 metres tall. On the ruler that is 10⁰ m, one metre. Every step up the ruler makes the view ten times wider.
Ten times bigger, then ten again. A blue whale, the Space Shuttle Endeavour, the Statue of Liberty and a Saturn V rocket: 10² m, a hundred metres.
The Burj Khalifa, the tallest building on Earth: 828 m, almost 10³ m, one kilometre (km).
Mount Everest, 8,848.86 m. Airliners cruise barely above its summit. We have reached 10⁴ m.
Los Angeles at night, from Santa Monica Bay to the harbour at San Pedro: about 100 km, or 10⁵ m.
The International Space Station (ISS) circles 410 km up, just above the thin glowing skin of the atmosphere. Space begins surprisingly close.
Earth: 12,742 km across, 10⁷ m. In one second, light could race around it seven and a half times.
The Moon is 30 Earths away. Light takes 1.3 seconds to get there; the Apollo astronauts took three days.
The Sun, 109 Earths wide. The light warming you today left its surface 8 minutes and 19 seconds ago.
Earth's orbit. The distance to the Sun, 150 million km, is the astronomical unit (AU): 10¹¹ m.
Some stars are vastly larger. The red hypergiant VY Canis Majoris would swallow every planet out to Jupiter.
All eight planets, where they are today. Neptune circles 30 AU out; its sunlight is 4 hours old.
Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is the most distant human-made object. In November 2026 its radio signals take a whole day to reach us.
One light-year: 9.46 trillion km, 10¹⁶ m. Even Voyager 1 has covered less than 0.3% of it.
The nearest stars, Alpha Centauri, 4.37 light-years away. Between here and there: almost nothing.
Star clusters and nebulae: the Orion Nebula and the Pleiades, tens of light-years across and hundreds away.
Our galaxy, the Milky Way: 100,000 light-years and hundreds of billions of stars. The Sun is one of them, out in a spiral arm.
Andromeda, 2.5 million light-years away. Its light left before there were any humans to see it.
The Local Group: two big spirals and dozens of dwarf galaxies, about 10 million light-years across.
The Laniakea Supercluster: 100,000 galaxies, all streaming toward the Great Attractor. 10²⁴ m.
Now galaxies are specks. They trace a cosmic web of filaments and voids, spun by gravity over 13.8 billion years.
The edge of what we can see: the observable universe, 93 billion light-years across. Its edge glows with the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB), light from 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
Now all the way back down, past where we started…
A grain of sand, half a millimetre: 10⁻⁴ m. Everything from here down is too small to see with your eyes.
Red blood cells, 8 micrometres (µm) across. You have about 25 trillion.
A virus is smaller than a wavelength of visible light. To see it we need electron microscopes.
DNA, the double helix, 2 nanometres (nm) wide: 10⁻⁹ m.
A hydrogen atom: a cloud of probability, 0.1 nm across. Almost all of it is empty space.
The proton at its heart, 10⁻¹⁵ m. From here to the edge of the observable universe: 42 powers of ten.
